Pregnancy 
Antepartum Risks
NRBS 3410
Summer 2026

Spontaneous Abortion
• Cause unknown and highly variable
• 1st trimester commonly due to fetal genetic 
abnormalities
• 2nd trimester more likely related to maternal 
conditions
• Nursing Assessment
• Vaginal bleeding
• Cramping or contractions
• Vital signs, pain level
• Client’s understanding

Bleeding Disorders in Early Pregnancy- Abortion
• Spontaneous Abortion/Miscarriage (AB)
 Expulsion of fetus prior to 20wks or <500g
 Risk in known pregnancy: 10-12%
• Threatened Abortion (threatened AB)
• Cervix is closed, bleeding and cramping.
• Inevitable-Bleeding, 
• Internal cervical os dilates
• Complete-ALL products of conception (POC)expelled.
• Incomplete-Retained POC-most often placenta.
• Missed-Fetus dies in Utero signs of pregnancy regress. If retained 
beyond 6 weeks may progress to DIC.
• Recurrent/Habitual-AB with 3 or more consecutive pregnancies.
• Risk of Septic-Infection increases if IUD is present or Prolonged 
Rupture of Membranes

Signs Symptoms and 
Nursing Care
• Cramping and backache-Pain Management.
• Ultrasound to evaluated presence/absence of FHR or Gestational Sac- 
Anticipatory Guidance.
• Bed Rest and Pelvic Rest.
• CBC to assess blood loss.
• IV Hydration or Blood Products if Necessary.
• D & C if POC are not expelled.
• Rhogam is Rh negative and not sensitized.

Care of Family 
• Evolving Process
 Disbelief with onset of symptoms
 Guilt-related to initial ambivalence.
 Grieving process may be as long as 2 yrs.
• Comfort Care
 What not to say is more important.
 Information regarding cause.
 Presence of Self.
 Support Groups/Referrals.

Ectopic Pregnancy 
non/extra-intrauterine pregnancy (IUP)
• Implantation of Fertilized Egg at site other than endometrial 
lining of uterus.
 Usually a Fallopian Tube Structure Issue
* Hx of Pelvic Inflammatory Disease
*Previous Tubal Surgery.
*Congenital Anomalies.
• Other Causes
*Endometriosis (proliferation of endometrial tissue outside uterine 
lining)
*IUD
*History of previous Ectopic.
*DES Exposure in Utero
Ectopic Pregnancy

Ectopic Pregnancy Cont’
• Incidence- 2% of pregnancies
• Initial S/S may mimic normal pregnancy
 Breast tenderness/hCG/amenorrhea/nausea
 Progresses, may rupture = bleeding in peritoneum.
• S/S rupture sharp one-side pain/syncope/shoulder pain.
• Dx-LMP/Pelvic Exam/Ultrasound/Hormone levels 
Progesterone < 25ng/ml (IUP =>25ng/ml)
hCG don’t double every 48-72° (IUP do)
• Tx- Methotrexate –non ruptured or Sx-ruptured 
Nursing care: Anticipatory Guidance
   Pain Assessment/Management
   Monitor S/S Bleeding

Ectopic Pregnancy (cont’d.)
• Nursing Management
• Preparation for treatment
• Analgesics for pain
• Medications for medical treatment
• Teaching about signs and symptoms of rupture
• Surgery if needed
• Emotional support 
• Education regarding post treatment period

Gestational Trophoblastic Disease (GTD)
• Two types
• Hydatidiform mole 
• Caused when an un-nucleated egg is fertilized
• Choriocarcinoma
• Malignancy of placental (trophoblastic tissue)
• 50% will follow a molar pregnancy
• 25% will follow a spontaneous abortion
• 25% will follow a normal pregnancy
• Exact cause unknown

Gestational Trophoblastic Disease 
GTD
• Pathologic proliferation of trophoblastic cells.
(outermost layer of embryonic cells)
• Hydatidaform Mole/Molar Pregnancy
1-placenta grows into grape like clusters.
   2-trophoblastic proliferation. 
 Risk for choriocarcinoma from trophoblastic cells.
 s/s- vaginal bleeding, uterus>or< dates, pre-eclampsia, 
• Tx- D & C and or methotrexate
• Nursing Care- Anticipatory Guidance, S/S bleeding/Support
• Long-term follow-up and monitoring of serial hCG 
levels for Choriocarinoma

Gestational Trophoblastic Disease
• Nursing Assessment 
• Clinical manifestations similar to spontaneous abortion at 12 weeks
• Ultrasound visualization of empty  
• Higher than expected hCG levels 
• Normal pregnancy beta hCG doubles every 72 hours until 10-12 wks
• Beta hCG then levels off and begins to fall as placenta takes over
• See chart next slide
• Nursing Management
• Preoperative preparation
• Emotional support
• Education: treatment, serial hCG monitoring, prophylactic 
chemotherapy
Beta HCG Levels: Molar vs Normal Pregnancy

Cervical Insufficiency/Incompetent Cervix
• Premature dilation of cervix usually in 4-5 month.
• Cause unknown; possibly due to cervical damage
• Cervical trauma, infection, uterine anomaly, multiples
• Hx of repeated 2nd trimester abortions
• Dx- shortened cervix on transvaginal US (< 3cms )
• Therapeutic Management
• Bed rest, pelvic rest, avoidance of heavy lifting
• Cervical cerclage in early pregnancy (before 20 wks)
 Tx- Cerclage-purse string suturing of cervix
    removed at term or delivery.

Cervical Insufficiency (cont’d.)
• Nursing Assessment
• Risk factors
• Pink-tinged vaginal discharge or pelvic pressure
• Hx: Cervical shortening via transvaginal ultrasound 
• Nursing Management
• Continuing surveillance; close monitoring for preterm labor
• Emotional support
• Education-signs of preterm labor

Hyperemesis Gravidarum
• Hyperemesis Gravidarum: Excessive Vomiting in Preg.
Theory: hCG, elevated levels of helicobacter pylori,
hypo function of thyroid, anterior pituitary, adrenal cortex.
 Risk- dehydration and metabolic imbalances
 Tx- IV hydration usually with K+ .  
 Severe cases may require parenteral nutrition (TPN)

Placenta Previa
• Cause unknown; placenta implants over cervical os
• Classification (see Figure 21.6)
• Therapeutic Management: dependent on bleeding, 
amount of placenta over os, fetal development and 
position, maternal parity, labor signs and symptoms
• Nursing Assessment
• Risk factors
• Vaginal bleeding (painless, bright red in 2nd or 3rd 
trimester, spontaneous cessation then recurrence)

Placenta Previa (cont’d.)
• Nursing Management
• Monitoring of maternal–fetal status
• Vaginal bleeding; pad count
• Avoidance of vaginal exams
• FHR
• Support and education: fetal movement counts, 
effects of prolonged bed rest (if necessary); signs 
and symptoms to report
• Preparation for possible cesarean birth (see pg. 
641 for emergent C/S)

Abruptio Placentae
• Separation of placenta during pregnancy leading 
to compromised fetal blood supply
• Etiology unknown
• Therapeutic Management: 
• Assessment
• Early Identification (bleeding may be concealed)
• Monitor Labs & V/S for changes
• STAT C/S
• Control and restoration of hemostatis
• Prevention of DIC 
IUGRIUGR

Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation
DIC incidence is greatest in:
 Intrauterine Fetal Demise (IUFD)
 Preeclampsia
 Abruptio Placentae
 Maternal Hepatic Disease
 Septic Abortion
Over activation of clotting process.
 Imbalance between coagulation (clotting) and fibrinolytic (clot dissolving) 
factors.
Hemorrhage and Clotting at the same time. Clots are formed and deposit 
in vasculature cause infarcts and elevated fibrin-fibrinogen degradation 
by-products lead to more bleeding.

Abruptio Placentae (cont’d.)
• Nursing Assessment 
• Risk factors-previous placental abruption
• High blood pressure
• Trauma
• Advanced maternal age
• Multiple pregnancis
• Cocaine use
• Symptoms
• Bleeding if present (dark red)
• Pain (knife-like), uterine tenderness, 
contractions
• Fetal movement and activity (decreased)
• FHR-decreased
• Laboratory and diagnostic testing: CBC, fibrinogen 
levels, PT/aPTT, type and cross-match, nonstress 
test, biophysical profile

Abruptio Placentae (cont’d.)
• Nursing Management
• Tissue perfusion
• left lateral position
• strict bed rest
• oxygen therapy
• vital signs
• continuous fetal monitoring
• Support and education
• empathy & understanding
• possible loss of fetus

Premature Rupture of Membranes: PROM/PPROM
• Spontaneous rupture of membranes before onset of labor.  
Associated with:
 Infection            Amniocentesis    Placenta Previa
 Hydramnios     Multiples   UTI
 Abrutio Placenta  Trauma               Incompetent Cervix
• PPROM = ROM  before  37 weeks.
 Maternal Risk= Chorioaminionitis (infection of amnion) 
 Endometritis (infection) post partum.
Fetal Risk= Infection: sepsis, RDS, cord prolapse.
• Increased morbidity and mortality.

Tx and Nursing Care PROM and PPROM
• Dx is via sterile speculum exam of cervix = + amniotic fluid in vagina 
• + nitrazine test 
• Normal vaginal secretions are acidic (pH 4.5–6.0). Amniotic fluid is more alkaline (pH 7.1–7.3).
Treatment
• Tx-Before 37 weeks=Bed Rest, Non-stress Test & Biophysical Profile
• Betamethasone (>32wks) Promotes surfactant production (matures fetal lungs)
Nsg: 
Admitted to Antepartum to bring pregnancy as close to term as possible
Vitals q 4°, FHR via Electronic Fetal Monitoring min. q 4° (may be continuous however if < 28wks not reliable)
Abx: to prevent infection.  
If leak is small/amnion repairs itself and fluid is stabile may d/c home for monitoring
d/c teaching= PELVIC REST, s/s infection, foul vaginal d/c or fetal movement return to L&D immediately.
After 37 weeks= Assess fetal well being  Abx therapy & Birth (may induce if no spontaneous)
• Most women with PROM will go into labor spontaneously within 24 hours.
• Risk for infection increases if not delivered by 24 hours
Nursing Care
• anticipatory guidance
• monitor for S/S maternal infection
• assess fetal well being

PTL : Preterm Labor
• Labor between 20-37 weeks.
 Prematurity = Greatest risk to baby.
 11% of infants are premature (MOD 2003)
• Early s/s may be confused with normal discomforts of pregnancy
 Predictors: History of PTL
Shortened Cervical Length
Bacterial Vaginosis
UTI
Diagnosed by:+ Uterine Contractions= 4/20min or 8/hour.
     + Cervical shortening and or dilation.
• Treatment: Stop progression of Labor.
 Tocolysis: medications to stop labor by suppressing uterine  contractions.
Beta adrenegeric agonists-Terbutaline most comm
See Nursing & Interprofessional Care Box 21.7

Outpatient PTL
• OUT-Patient Education of Signs Symptoms
 Uterine contractions q 10 min or less.
 ROM or change in vaginal discharge.
 Abdominal pain without diarrhea
 Menstrual like cramping.
 Management of patient on Magnesium Sulfate.
 Administer corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity.
• Teach Self Care Measures to Prevent:
 Rest: Left side lying 2-3x day avoid exertion.
 Stay hydrated: 2-3 quarts H2O daily.
 May need to stop sexual activity.
 Emotional Support.

Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy
• Preeclampsia: Onset of hypertension after 20 weeks accompanied by proteinuria.
• Most common hypertensive problem in pregnancy 3-7% nulliparas 0.8% of multiparas. 
• Greatest incidence: Teens and >35yrs. 
• Greatest Risk: First pregnancy or first pregnancy with FOB.
• Unknown etiology effecting multiple organ systems.
 HTN: Theory: The normalperipheral vascular resistance found of pregnancy is related to 
increased production of Nitric Oxide a vasodialator influenced by  placental hormonal 
production. Beginning at 20 weeks there is aNitric oxide (vasodilator) in women with 
preeclampsia.
 Vascular spasm can occur that may be caused increased intravascular volume required by 
pregnancy, which injures the endothelial cells of the arteries and reduces the action of 
prostacyclin—a prostaglandin vasodilator—and excess production of thromboxane—a 
prostaglandin vasoconstrictor and stimulant of platelet aggregation.
 Proteinuria: increased perfusion (GFR) = increase extra cellular volume of the glomerular 
endothelium= Stretching of capillary walls
=LARGE PARTICLES OF ALBUMIN ESCAPING INTO URINE.
May progress to Eclampsia= Seizure or Coma

Preeclampsia Signs Symptoms 
Mild: Few if any symptoms.  Edema of face and or hands or 
wt gain of ≥3.3lbs month in 2nd trimester
Dx-Increased B/P ≥ 140/90 
proteinuria is between 300mg/L – 1g/L    
(+1 to +2) on urine dip stick.
Severe: Visual disturbances, N/V, RUQ pain/epigastric 
pain, hyperreflexia, IUGR, thrombocytopenia.
Dx-B/P 160/110 on 2 occasions 
6° apart while on bed rest.
Proteinuria ≥ 5g in a 24-hour urine collection or (+3 
to +4 )2 times 4° apart. Oliguria ≤500ml/24°

Preeclampsia
• Maternal Risk: CNS changes, hyperreflexia, can progress to HELLP Syndrome or 
eclampsia.
- Can occur post-partum.
• Fetal Risk: SGA related to maternal vasospasm     and hypovolemia.
     Risk of Premature Birth.
    Hypermagnesemia r/t maternal
    Magnesium Sulfate therapy.

Treatment Preeclampsia = Delivery 
Mild: May be managed at home (severity)
Bed rest
High Protein Diet
Anti-hypertensives for B/P
Severe: In-patient bed-rest, I & O, diet modifications and anti-
hypertensives.
Magnesium Sulfate to prevent seizures.
-Loading dose= 6g/100ml IV over 20 min.
-maintenance dose= 2g/hr IV
Target Therapeutic Level = 4.8-9.6mg/dl
 DTR @ 8-12mg/dl
Resp @ 15-17mg/dl
Cardiac Arrest @>30mg/dl

Nursing Management/Assessment 
• Bed Rest
• Q 8° Labs.
• Frequent VS (q1-4h) with FHR/often continuous EFM.
• Neuro checks: Symptoms may be S/E meds.
• Dizziness
• LOC 
• DTR’s :hyperreflexia=+3 DTR
• Headache – CNS irritability)
• Visual changes – blurry, spots (retinal artery spasm)
• Respiratory Assessment for Pulmonary Edema.
• Strict I & O and Daily Wts.

Eclampsia = Seizure
• Medical Emergency
• Managed by Magnesium Sulfate IV 4-6g over 5 minutes.  
• Sedatives given in Mag doesn’t work.
• Pt assessed for Pulmonary Edema, Renal Failure, Cerebral 
Hemorrhage.
• Induction of Labor if fetus is viable.
• Corticosteroids if within window 30-35wks.

HELLP SYNDROME
HELLP Syndrome: Indicates more severe preeclampsia (high 
morbidity and mortality):
• Hemolysis – arterial spasm causes endothelial damage – rbc forced 
through and causes hemolysis and hyperbilirubinemia 
• Elevated Liver Enzymes – hepatic involvement, microemboli in 
hepatic vasculature (know normal liver function tests ALT/AST)
• ALT =7 to 55 units per liter (U/L)
• AST =8 to 48 U/L
• Low Platelets – increase in consumption because plts aggregate at 
damaged endothelium sites <150,000 µL (microliter)
DIC – even more severe/advanced stage
• Coagulation cascade activated
Seizures

Other Hypertensive Disorders
• Chronic Hypertension: pre 20weeks or pre-pregnancy or after 42nd day Post-
partum
• Treatment goal is to prevent preeclampsia.
• Chronic HTN w/ super-imposed preeclampsia: 25% of women with Chronic HTN 
get preeclampsia
• Gestational or Transient HTN: After 20 weeks without proteinuria or PIH 
(Pregnancy Induced HTN).

Disseminated Intravascular 
Coagulation
DIC incidence is greatest in:
 Intrauterine Fetal Demise (IUFD)
 Preeclampsia
 Abruptio Placentae
 Maternal Hepatic Disease
 Septic Abortion
Over activation of clotting process.
 Imbalance between coagulation (clotting) and fibrinolytic (clot dissolving) 
factors.
Hemorrhage and Clotting at the same time. Clots are formed deposit in 
vasculature cause infarcts and elevated fibrin-fibrinogen degradation by-
products lead to more bleeding.

Rh Incompatibility/Alloimmunization
• Rh   mother with Rh ̄ + baby.
Mother is sensitized to Rh antigen and forms anti-bodies 
against Rh factor.
If 1st baby-may not be an issue 2nd pregnancy is at risk for 
hemolytic disorder.
Rh neg mom= Antibody screening (indirect Coombs test) at 
1st visit.
Repeat at 28wks- positive= sensitization.
Rhogam-Rh immune globulin given at 28 wks if indirect 
Coombs negative.  
Given after delivery, after abortion.
Rh Incompatibility/Alloimmunization

Prevention
• Accomplished by passive immunization with anti-D antibody 
given to those women with negative antibody screens
• Term gestation-standard dose of RhoGam (300 mcg) is given at 
28 weeks EGA & 2nd dose is given within 72 hrs of delivery-
reduces risk of sensitization from 16% to 2%, residual 2% risk is 
likely from sensitization during pregnancy
• Doesn’t work perfectly, risk reduced to 1 in 1000
• Protects against transfusion of 15ml of fetal’s RBC or 30 ml of 
fetal blood
• MICRogam is used for 1st trimester abortion/miscarriage, 50 
mcg, protects against transfusion of 2.5 ml of fetal blood
• Anti-D antibody originates from plasma of individuals with high 
titers all plasma lots are tested for HIV, hepatitis B & C, 
processing removes all viral particles 
Casanova, R., er at. (2019). Beckmann and Ling’ s Obstetrics and Gynecology 8th Ed:  New York, NY , Wolters Kuwer

ABO Incompatibility
• Essentially same principle as Rh incompatibility
• Occurs in 20-25% of pregnancies.
• Rarely causes hemolytic syndromes.
• No post-partum treatment.

T-O-R-S-C-H Infections
• Toxoplasmosis – Protozoa found in raw meat and cat feces.  1st 
trimester=lowest rate of fetal infection but highest severity and 
death.
• Rubella – German Measles Virus. severe anomalies; vaccinate 
before or after pregnancy. Titers drawn at 1st prenatal visit.
• Syphilis- STI if left untreated can cross placenta @ 16-18 
weeks and cause cognitive or hearing problems and 
fetal death
• Cytomegalovirus (CMV)- herpes family- fatal to fetus
• Herpes Simplex– No intrauterine infection risk is at delivery. 
Antivirals ok in pregnancy but if active lesions=C-section. 50% 
infant mortality rate if infected at birth and untreated.

Physical Abuse in Pregnancy
• Intimate Partner Violence (IPV): 4-8% of pregnant women.
• Increases pregnancy complications.
• Abuse screening is every nurse’s responsibility.  On-going 
assessment. 
Ask at 1st visit, each visit and post-partum.
1-800-621-HOPE = NYC IPV Helpline
1-800-799-SAFE = National IPV Helpline
Establish Trust: Increase woman’s decision-making ability to 
help herself and her children.

Group B Streptococcus
• Normal flora of lower GI and Utero-genital tracts.  
• Risk is to neonate: infected during childbirth either by 
ascending bacteria with ROM or by direct contact in canal.
• Neonate Sepsis, Pneumonia, Meningitis
• Mother is tested at 35-37 weeks
Vaginal/rectal swab.
• Treated with Abx at onset of labor or ROM
• Pennicillin G at least 4 hours before.
• Every 4 hours until birth
• Newborn will be monitored for signs of infection
• Symptomatic newborns will get sepsis workup
• Previous hx of GBS=treatment at every birth.

Amniotic Fluid Disorders
• Amniotic fluid is dynamic-large volumes flowing in and out of the amniotic 
compartment everyday
• AFI is not absolutely true predictor of volume
• Amniotic fluid needed for fetal lung development
• In an IUGR or post dates pregnancy oligohydramnios is associated with a 
significant increase in perinatal morbidity and mortality
• Isolated olighydramnios in preterm or term pregnancies is not associated 
with increased perinatal morbidity or mortality with an otherwise normal 
fetus
• Early onset or severe polyhydramnios is associated with chromosomal 
abnormalities, congenital malformations, preterm delivery and perinatal 
mortality

Amniotic Fluid
• Main source of AF is fetal urine
• 1000-1200 mL/day is produced at term
• The entire AFV is replaced more frequently than every 
24 hours
• Fetal lung fluid also plays an important role in AF 
formation
• Fetal swallowing occurs from very early on and 
contributes to removal of AF  
• Intermembranous absorption- for removal of fluid

Oligohydramnios
• Oligohydramnios-AFV of less than of 200-500 mL
• Amniotic fluid index, (AFI) of less than 5 cm.  Maximum 
vertical pocket (MVP) less than 2 cm
• Causes-renal agenesis, obstructed uropathy, PROM, 
abnormal placentation, prolonged pregnancy, severe IUGR
• Maternal conditions-dehydration, hypertensive disorders, 
uteroplacental insufficiency, antiphospholipid syndrome
• Dx made on ultrasound 
• Evaluate for IUGR
• Antepartum testing

Oligohydramnios
•Obtain hx and physical- 2nd trimester
•R/O ruptured membranes
•Usg- evaluate anatomy, growth
•Increase maternal fluids
•Left lateral position

Polyhydramnios
• AFI of 25 or greater, ONE MVP greater than 8
• Severe cases in 2nd and 3rd trimesters significant perinatal 
mortality rate (PMR) due to prematurity or aneuploidy
• Dx by ultrasound
• Can be treated by indomethacin
• Causes-GI obstruction, CNS anomalies, aneuploidy, genetic 
disorders, twin to twin transfusion, infections (parvovirus), 
placental abnormalities
• Maternal-idiopathic, poorly controlled DM, feto-maternal 
hemorrhage
• Majority in 3rd trimester are idiopathic

Complications
• Preterm delivery 
• Preeclampsia 
• IUFD 
• Neonatal demise
• Placental abruption
• Postpartum hemorrhage
• Uterine dysfunction

Polyhydramnios
• USG for fetal anatomy
• NST, kick counts, BPP
• Short term use of indomethacin decreases fetal urine 
production and can cause decrease AFV within 24 
hours. Prolonged use should be avoided because of 
premature closure of the ductus arteriosus & renal 
abnormalities in the newborn
• Amnioreductions- removal of amniotic fluid

Polyhydramnios (Hydramnios)
• Amniotic fluid >2,000 mL 
• Associated with fetal abnormalities
• Maternal Risk-GDM, DM, infection, multiples
• Therapeutic Management: close monitoring; removal 
of fluid (therapeutic amniocentis), indomethacin 
(decreases fluid by decreasing fetal urinary output)
• Nursing Assessment: fundal height, abdominal 
discomfort, difficulty palpating fetal parts or 
obtaining FHR
• Nursing Management: ongoing assessment and 
monitoring; assisting with therapeutic amniocentesis

Oligohydramnios
• Amniotic fluid <500 mL
• Therapeutic Management: serial monitoring; 
amnioinfusion and birth for fetal compromise
• Nursing Assessment: risk factors, fluid leaking 
from vagina
• Nursing Management: continuous fetal 
surveillance; assistance with amnioinfusion, 
comfort measures, position changes

Multiple Gestation
• Therapeutic management: serial ultrasounds, 
close monitoring during labor, operative delivery 
(common)
• Nursing Assessment: uterus larger than 
expected for EDB; ultrasound confirmation 
• Nursing Management: education and support 
antepartally; labor management with perinatal 
team on standby; postpartum assessment for 
possible hemorrhage
